newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodian premier says to cooperate with rival.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian premier says to cooperate with rival.

text.p: Cambodia's First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh was quoted on Saturday as saying he would cooperate with his rival Hun Sen for the sake of peace and economic development in the turbulent country.

A Cambodian official said Ranariddh told this to Thai premier Chavalit Yongchaiyudh, who flew in to Phnom Penh earlier on Saturday for a 24-hour visit during which he was expected to express concern over Cambodia's simmering political crisis.
Diplomats in Phnom Penh said Chavalit had been expected to urge the two joint leaders to resolve their differences as Cambodia prepared to join the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN).

"Prince Ranariddh told Chavalit...he will cooperate with Second Prime Minister Hun Sen to make peace and political stability for Cambodia and for investment," Nady Tan, secretary general of Cambodia's Council of Ministers, told reporters.
Cambodia, Burma and Laos are due next month to become full members of ASEAN, which currently groups Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.
Chavalit's visit came as international concern grew over escalating political violence in Cambodia.
Bodyguards loyal to the two premiers fought a brief but fierce street battle in Phnom Penh on Tuesday night which left two dead.

A long-running power-struggle between Ranariddh and Hun Sen, which is at the heart of their feud, intensified in recent weeks with the collapse of the Khmer Rouge guerrilla group and bitter disagreement over how to handle the remnants of the rebel army.
Chavalit, who met the two leaders for talks earlier, declined to comment on Saturday's announcement that hated Khmer Rouge leader Pol Pot had been captured in remote jungle of northern Cambodia.
Pol Pot and his Khmer Rouge guerrilla force have long been a thorn in relations between the neighbouring countries.

Thailand was a key supporter of the Khmer Rouge, royalist forces and another non-communist guerrilla group during the 1980s when the guerrilla alliance battled a Vietnamese army of occupation and the Hanoi-backed government in Phnom Penh.

Although all outside powers agreed to cease support for the Cambodian factions after a 1991 peace treaty, Cambodian military leaders have repeatedly accused Thailand of assisting the Khmer Rouge in their remote bases near the Thai border.
Chavalit signed a border trade and cultural cooperation pacts with his Cambodian counterparts on Saturday, Cambodian government officials said.

Cambodia also asked Thailand to help curb the smuggling of timber from Cambodian forests into Thailand. The two countries agreed to work together in the areas of health, human resources and the fight against narcotics smuggling, the officials said.
